# Acupoints

> A free, modern reference for the 361 WHO-standardized acupoints — organized by meridian, body region, and everyday concern.

Acupoints documents all 361 classical acupressure points in plain English: every point page carries the WHO-standard location, dataset-recorded indications and cautions, and sources; editorial pages add how-to-find steps, FAQs, and deeper guidance. The site is educational and is not medical advice.

## Points

- [LI4 Hegu](https://acupoints.com/en/points/li4/): LI4 (Hegu) is a hand acupoint on the Large Intestine meridian, classically used for headache, facial pain, and immune support; it is contraindicated in pregnancy.
- [PC6 Neiguan](https://acupoints.com/en/points/pc6/): PC6 (Neiguan) is a forearm acupoint on the Pericardium meridian, classically used for nausea, motion sickness, anxiety, and palpitations.
- [ST36 Zusanli](https://acupoints.com/en/points/st36/): ST36 (Zusanli) is a lower-leg acupoint on the Stomach meridian, classically considered a point of general vitality — used for digestion, fatigue, and immune support.
- [GB20 Fengchi](https://acupoints.com/en/points/gb20/): GB20 (Fengchi) is a neck acupoint on the Gallbladder meridian, classically used for headache, neck tension, eye strain, and early cold symptoms.
- [SP6 Sanyinjiao](https://acupoints.com/en/points/sp6/): SP6 (Sanyinjiao) is an inner-leg acupoint where three yin meridians meet, used for menstrual and digestive concerns; it is contraindicated in pregnancy.
- [LV3 Taichong](https://acupoints.com/en/points/lv3/): LV3 (Taichong) is a foot acupoint on the Liver meridian, classically used for stress, irritability, headache, and menstrual discomfort.
- [GV20 Baihui](https://acupoints.com/en/points/gv20/): GV20 (Baihui) is a crown-of-the-head acupoint on the Governing Vessel, classically used to lift mood, clear the mind, and anchor scattered attention.
- [CV17 Danzhong](https://acupoints.com/en/points/cv17/): CV17 (Danzhong) is a chest acupoint on the Conception Vessel, classically used for tightness in the chest, breath, and grief.
- [HT7 Shenmen](https://acupoints.com/en/points/ht7/): HT7 (Shenmen) is a wrist acupoint on the Heart meridian, classically used for anxiety, insomnia, and a racing mind.
- [LU7 Lieque](https://acupoints.com/en/points/lu7/): LU7 (Lieque) is a forearm acupoint on the Lung meridian, classically used for head and neck complaints, coughs, and early colds.
- [KI3 Taixi](https://acupoints.com/en/points/ki3/): KI3 (Taixi) is an inner-ankle acupoint on the Kidney meridian, classically used for fatigue, low back ache, tinnitus, and night sweats.
- [BL40 Weizhong](https://acupoints.com/en/points/bl40/): BL40 (Weizhong) is a back-of-knee acupoint on the Bladder meridian, classically used for low back pain and stiffness.
- [BL57 Chengshan](https://acupoints.com/en/points/bl57/): BL57 (Chengshan) is a calf acupoint on the Bladder meridian, classically used for calf cramps, heel pain, and lower back strain.
- [SI3 Houxi](https://acupoints.com/en/points/si3/): SI3 (Houxi) is a hand acupoint on the Small Intestine meridian, classically used for neck stiffness, upper back tension, and headache.
- [TH5 Waiguan](https://acupoints.com/en/points/th5/): TH5 (Waiguan) is a forearm acupoint on the San Jiao meridian, classically used for head and side-of-neck complaints, ear issues, and wrist pain.
- [ST44 Neiting](https://acupoints.com/en/points/st44/): ST44 (Neiting) is a foot acupoint on the Stomach meridian, classically used for toothache, facial pain, and heat in the stomach.
- [SP9 Yinlingquan](https://acupoints.com/en/points/sp9/): SP9 (Yinlingquan) is an inner-leg acupoint on the Spleen meridian, classically used for digestive heaviness, water retention, and knee discomfort.
- [LI11 Quchi](https://acupoints.com/en/points/li11/): LI11 (Quchi) is an elbow acupoint on the Large Intestine meridian, classically used for heat, skin complaints, and arm pain.
- [GV14 Dazhui](https://acupoints.com/en/points/gv14/): GV14 (Dazhui) is an upper-back acupoint on the Governing Vessel, classically used for neck stiffness, early colds, and heat.
- [EX-HN5 Taiyang](https://acupoints.com/en/points/ex-hn5/): Taiyang (EX-HN5) is a temple acupoint outside the twelve regular meridians, classically used for headache, eye strain, and facial tension.
- [LU1 Zhongfu](https://acupoints.com/en/points/lu1/): LU1 (Zhongfu) is an acupoint on the Lung meridian, classically used for cough, asthma, and chest fullness and pain.

## Meridians

- [Lung](https://acupoints.com/en/meridians/lung/): The Lung meridian runs from the chest down the inner arm to the thumb and governs respiration and the body’s defensive qi.
- [Large Intestine](https://acupoints.com/en/meridians/large-intestine/): The Large Intestine meridian runs from the index finger up the arm to the face and is classically used for headache, facial pain, and immunity.
- [Stomach](https://acupoints.com/en/meridians/stomach/): The Stomach meridian runs down the front of the body from face to second toe and is classically used for digestion, energy, and appetite.
- [Spleen](https://acupoints.com/en/meridians/spleen/): The Spleen meridian ascends from the big toe up the inner leg to the chest, governing digestion, blood, and women’s health.
- [Heart](https://acupoints.com/en/meridians/heart/): The Heart meridian runs from the armpit down the inner arm to the little finger and houses the shen, or spirit.
- [Small Intestine](https://acupoints.com/en/meridians/small-intestine/): The Small Intestine meridian travels from the little finger up the arm to the face and is used for neck, shoulder, and ear conditions.
- [Bladder](https://acupoints.com/en/meridians/bladder/): The Bladder meridian runs from the inner eye over the head and down the back to the little toe and is the longest meridian in the body.
- [Kidney](https://acupoints.com/en/meridians/kidney/): The Kidney meridian ascends from the sole of the foot up the inner leg to the chest, rooting the body’s foundational qi.
- [Pericardium](https://acupoints.com/en/meridians/pericardium/): The Pericardium meridian runs from the chest down the inner arm to the middle finger and is a primary circuit for nausea and anxiety.
- [San Jiao](https://acupoints.com/en/meridians/san-jiao/): The San Jiao (Triple Burner) meridian runs from the ring finger up the outer arm to the temple and coordinates the three body cavities.
- [Gallbladder](https://acupoints.com/en/meridians/gallbladder/): The Gallbladder meridian zigzags down the side of the head and body to the fourth toe and is classically used for tension and decision-making.
- [Liver](https://acupoints.com/en/meridians/liver/): The Liver meridian rises from the big toe up the inner leg to the ribs and is used to soothe irritability, stagnation, and women’s cycles.
- [Du (Governing Vessel)](https://acupoints.com/en/meridians/du/): The Du or Governing Vessel runs up the midline of the back and head, uniting all yang meridians.
- [Ren (Conception Vessel)](https://acupoints.com/en/meridians/ren/): The Ren or Conception Vessel runs up the midline of the front of the body, uniting all yin meridians.

## Conditions

- [Tension headache](https://acupoints.com/en/conditions/tension-headache/): Tension headache is a dull, band-like pain across the forehead or base of the skull; classical acupressure points include LI4, GB20, and LV3.
- [Anxiety](https://acupoints.com/en/conditions/anxiety/): For mild anxiety, classical acupressure reaches for points like HT7, PC6, and Yintang — typically alongside slow breathing.
- [Travel nausea](https://acupoints.com/en/conditions/travel-nausea/): PC6 (Neiguan) on the inner forearm is the classical acupoint for travel and morning nausea and the point behind motion-sickness wristbands.
- [Insomnia](https://acupoints.com/en/conditions/insomnia/): For sleep, classical acupressure pairs a calming point at the wrist, HT7, with a grounding point on the sole, KI1.
- [Period pain](https://acupoints.com/en/conditions/period-pain/): For period pain, TCM most often draws on SP6, LV3, and local abdominal points — though some (like SP6) are avoided during pregnancy.
- [Back pain](https://acupoints.com/en/conditions/back-pain/): Classical acupressure for lower back pain often combines BL23, BL40, and GB30, chosen by where the pain is located.
- [Neck and shoulder strain from desk work](https://acupoints.com/en/conditions/desk-neck-shoulder/): Neck and shoulder strain from desk work eases first with breaks every hour or two, forearm support and neck exercise; classical acupressure adds GB20, GB21 and LI11 as an optional comfort pause, on limited evidence.
- [Nausea after surgery or chemotherapy](https://acupoints.com/en/conditions/nausea-after-treatment/): For nausea after surgery or chemotherapy, classical acupressure reaches first for PC6 (Neiguan) on the inner wrist, with LI4 and ST36 as companions — always as an add-on to prescribed anti-sickness medicine, never a replacement.
- [Bloating](https://acupoints.com/en/conditions/bloating/): For a bloated, distended belly, Chinese nursing care pairs clockwise belly massage with CV12, ST25 and CV6 on the abdomen and ST36 and PC6 on the leg and wrist; skip CV6 in pregnancy.
- [Constipation](https://acupoints.com/en/conditions/constipation/): For ordinary constipation, habits come first; classical acupressure adds a clockwise belly massage and the points ST25, TH6, ST36, and ST37.
- [Knee arthritis pain](https://acupoints.com/en/conditions/knee-arthritis/): For knee osteoarthritis pain, exercise and weight management come first; classical acupressure adds six points ringing the knee: SP10, ST34, ST35, SP9, GB34 and ST36.
- [After a stroke](https://acupoints.com/en/conditions/after-stroke-limbs/): After a stroke, a national Chinese nursing protocol names GB21, LI11, TH5 and LI4 on the arm and GB34, BL40 and GB39 on the leg; a carer presses them lightly on the weak side, alongside rehabilitation, never on spastic muscle or a swollen limb.
- [Fatigue](https://acupoints.com/en/conditions/fatigue/): For everyday tiredness of the depleted kind, Chinese medicine reaches for ST36 (Zusanli), SP6, CV6 and CV4 below the navel, and LI4; research on hand-pressed points comes mainly from fatigue after cancer treatment and in haemodialysis.
- [Labour pain](https://acupoints.com/en/conditions/labour-pain/): Sanyinjiao (SP6) and hegu (LI4), pressed by a birth partner through contractions, only once labour has started at 37 weeks or later and only with the midwife's or obstetric team's agreement; never to start labour or before term.

## Body regions

- [Head](https://acupoints.com/en/regions/head/): The head covers the scalp, face, and crown of the skull, where yang meridians converge and classical points for headache, eye strain, and clarity of mind are most concentrated.
- [Neck](https://acupoints.com/en/regions/neck/): The neck spans the region between the base of the skull and the shoulders, housing points classically used for neck stiffness, throat complaints, and the transition between head and body.
- [Shoulder](https://acupoints.com/en/regions/shoulder/): The shoulder spans the upper trapezius, the joint itself, and the tissue that connects neck to arm; its points are used for shoulder pain, restricted movement, and upper-body tension.
- [Chest](https://acupoints.com/en/regions/chest/): The chest covers the anterior thorax from the collarbones to the lower sternum, where Conception-Vessel and organ-front points relate to breath, heart, and emotional expression.
- [Back](https://acupoints.com/en/regions/back/): The back runs from the base of the neck to the sacrum and carries the Governing Vessel along the midline and the Bladder meridian down the paraspinal muscles, with points used for spinal tension, organ support, and overall vitality.
- [Arm](https://acupoints.com/en/regions/arm/): The arm runs from the shoulder joint to the wrist and carries six of the twelve regular meridians along its inner and outer surfaces; its points are used for head, chest, and digestive complaints as well as local arm issues.
- [Hand](https://acupoints.com/en/regions/hand/): The hand covers the wrist, palm, and fingers and is the distal terminus of the six arm meridians, hosting many accessible command points used for head, face, and systemic complaints.
- [Leg](https://acupoints.com/en/regions/leg/): The leg spans the hip to the ankle and carries six of the twelve regular meridians, with points along the shin, calf, and thigh used for digestion, back pain, and women’s health.
- [Foot](https://acupoints.com/en/regions/foot/): The foot is the distal terminus of the six leg meridians and hosts many yuan-source and well-points used for grounding, head and face complaints, and organ balance.
- [Ear](https://acupoints.com/en/regions/ear/): The ear is a microsystem in its own right, with points used for hearing, balance, and a broad range of auricular-therapy protocols; several regular meridians also skirt its margins.

## Basics

- [What is qi?](https://acupoints.com/en/basics/what-is-qi/): Qi (氣) in Traditional Chinese Medicine refers to the body’s capacity for coordinated movement and change — not a mystical energy, but a practical descriptor for function.
- [Yin and yang](https://acupoints.com/en/basics/yin-and-yang/): Yin and yang in TCM are descriptive lenses — not moral opposites — for tracking paired dynamics like cold/warm, quiet/active, interior/exterior.
- [The five elements](https://acupoints.com/en/basics/five-elements/): The five elements — wood, fire, earth, metal, water — are a classical relational model linking organs, emotions, and seasons.

## Glossary

- [De qi](https://acupoints.com/en/glossary/de-qi/): De qi (得氣) is the dull, heavy, or radiating sensation that signals a classical acupoint has been correctly located.
- [Yuan-source point](https://acupoints.com/en/glossary/yuan-source/): A yuan-source point is a classical “origin” point on each primary meridian, used to reach the organ it governs.
- [Cun](https://acupoints.com/en/glossary/cun/): Cun (寸) is a body-proportional unit of measurement used to locate acupoints, roughly the width of the patient’s own thumb at the knuckle.

## Journal

- [Cycle Comfort: A Period-Pain Routine at Home](https://acupoints.com/en/journal/cycle-comfort-routine/): When period pain arrives, most of us want two things at once: something kind to do with an evening, and honesty about what that evening can and cannot change. This guide offers a quiet at-home routine — warmth, slowed breathing, and two well-recorded classical points, Sanyinjiao (SP6) and Taichong (LV3) — together with the boundaries that keep home practice honest.
- [The Desk Worker’s Back: A Five-Minute Routine](https://acupoints.com/en/journal/desk-back-routine/): Eight hours in a chair asks plenty of a back and returns little. This piece answers the question most desk workers ask first — whether five minutes can help — then walks through a short routine built on two classical stations, Shenshu (BL23) at the small of the back and Weizhong (BL40) behind the knee, with desk habits, honest expectations, and clearly drawn stop lines alongside.
- [Getting Started with Acupressure](https://acupoints.com/en/journal/getting-started-with-acupressure/): Acupressure is the quiet art of pressing classical points with your fingers instead of needles. This guide covers what the practice is, where it comes from, how to find and press points gently, a three-point starter routine, and the safety lines every beginner should know.
- [Measuring With Your Own Hands: The Cun System](https://acupoints.com/en/journal/measuring-with-cun/): Classical locations read like riddles: two cun above the wrist, three below the knee. What is a cun, and where do you buy a ruler marked in them? You already own one. This guide explains the body-proportional system behind point location — finger measures, landmark tables, and the habit of measuring with your own hands.
- [Motion Sickness on the Road: A Traveller's Routine](https://acupoints.com/en/journal/motion-sickness-on-the-road/): Motion sickness has a famous address on the classical map: neiguan (PC6), on the inner forearm between two tendons. This post gives an honest answer to whether wrist pressure helps, a step-by-step routine to follow on a coach or a ferry, zusanli (ST36) as a companion point, and the safety lines worth keeping.
- [Pressure, Not Needles: What Self-Acupressure Is and Isn’t](https://acupoints.com/en/journal/pressure-not-needles/): Finger pressure asks almost nothing of you — no needles, no kit, no appointments — yet the line between home self-care and professional treatment is where beginners most often lose their footing. This guide sets out plainly what self-acupressure is, what it is not, and where the boundaries sit.
- [Steadier Days: Pressure Points for Anxious Spells](https://acupoints.com/en/journal/steadier-anxious-days/): Anxious spells visit everyone: the evening that will not quieten, the morning that starts already wound tight. This guide gathers a steady routine around two wrist points — shenmen (HT7) and neiguan (PC6), old companions of household tradition when the mind would not settle — covering how to find them, how to press them kindly, and where honest limits lie.
- [A Tension-Headache Toolkit for Ordinary Days](https://acupoints.com/en/journal/tension-headache-toolkit/): Tight bands across the forehead, a dull squeeze at the temples, heaviness pooling at the base of the skull — ordinary head tension knows how to claim an afternoon. This toolkit collects the four points traditional practice reached for most often, a five-minute routine for ordinary days, and the honest limits of finger-pressure self-care.
- [What De Qi Feels Like — and When to Stop](https://acupoints.com/en/journal/what-de-qi-feels-like/): Press the right spot and something curious happens: a deep, spreading heaviness quite unlike ordinary soreness. Tradition calls that feeling de qi. This guide explains what it is, how to invite it gently, what to make of a quiet day, and the clear moments that mean stop.
- [A Wind-Down Ritual for Sleepless Evenings](https://acupoints.com/en/journal/wind-down-for-sleep/): Some nights the lamp goes off and the mind stays at its desk. This guide offers a quiet ritual for such evenings — two classical points found by touch, a wrist gate and a sole spring, worked gently for about ten minutes, framed as tradition rather than treatment, and bounded by clear lines about when sleeplessness belongs with a clinician.
